html:
The Sápara are an Indigenous people of the Amazon rainforest of Ecuador and Peru, between the Napo and Pastaza rivers. Their language belongs to the small Zaparoan family.

In the 1700s they were one of the larger peoples of the region, but missions, epidemics and above all the rubber boom around 1900 brought them close to extinction. Many survivors married into the Kichwa and the language faded. In 2001 UNESCO named the Sápara language and culture a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, when only a few elders still spoke it. Today they defend their forest against oil drilling, alongside neighbours such as the Shuar.
